\chapter{Animals About the House --- Horse, Cow, Sheep, Hen, Donkey}
\label{ch:animales}
\hlchaptermodality{296}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the horse, the cow, the sheep, the hen and the donkey in Spanish.}

Complete ES-C296-burro: name all five animals in order, and say which one English took back off Spanish.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el caballo]{el caballo — the plodder that won}

\label{lesson:ES-C296-caballo}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what was \emph{insula}? (An island.) And what did \emph{nebula} mean, as against \emph{nubes}? (Mist, not cloud.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item perro — an animal you have had for a long time.
  \item gato — the other one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ca-BA-llo}, stress in the middle. The \emph{b} is soft between vowels, and the \emph{ll} is the \emph{y} of \emph{llueve}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el caballo} — \textquotedblleft{}the horse.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had two words for the animal. \textbf{Equus} was the horse of poetry and of the cavalry parade. \textbf{Caballus} was the other one: a plodding, thick-legged work-horse, close to \textquotedblleft{}nag.\textquotedblright{} Educated Romans wrote \emph{equus}.

And \emph{caballus} is the one that survived. Not just in Spanish — French \emph{cheval}, Italian \emph{cavallo}, Portuguese \emph{cavalo}. The polite word went into the museum and the stable word went into every mouth in western Europe.

English is full of the plodder without knowing it. \textbf{Cavalry} is soldiers on \emph{caballi}. A \textbf{cavalier} was one of them. And \textbf{chivalry} is the same word again, worn down through French — so the most elevated idea the Middle Ages had is named after a nag.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One animal, and a rule of thumb worth more than the animal.

When Latin had a grand word and a plain word for the same thing, bet on the plain one. That is what people actually said, and what people actually said is what became Spanish.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el caballo}
  \item \emph{el caballo} and \emph{el perro}, one after the other
  \item \emph{el caballo del pueblo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word won, \emph{equus} or \emph{caballus}? (\emph{Caballus}.) What kind of horse was it? (A plain work-horse.) And which English word for soldiers on horseback holds it? (\emph{Cavalry}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la vaca]{la vaca — the animal inside a medical word}

\label{lesson:ES-C296-vaca}



\begin{quote}
Two back: what did \emph{nebula} name? (The mist.) And which Latin horse won, the grand one or the plain one? (The plain one, \emph{caballus}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el caballo — the animal before this one.
  \item el queso — what this one is behind.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{VA-ca}, stress on the first part. The \emph{v} is the same sound as \emph{b}, and the \emph{c} before \emph{a} is hard. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la vaca} — \textquotedblleft{}the cow.\textquotedblright{}

There is almost nothing to take apart. Latin \textbf{vacca}, Spanish \emph{vaca}: one consonant thinned and the rest left alone. Some words travel two thousand years and arrive with their hat still on.

The interesting part is in English. In the seventeen-nineties Edward Jenner noticed that dairymaids who had caught cowpox did not catch smallpox, and he built a treatment on it. He named it from \textbf{vaccinus}, Latin for \textquotedblleft{}of the cow\textquotedblright{} — so \textbf{vaccine}, and every vaccine since, is named after this animal.

Nothing about a modern vaccine involves a cow. The name is a fossil of the first one, in the way \emph{la salida} is a fossil of somebody actually going out.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two animals, and a word English uses every day without knowing whose it is.

\emph{El caballo} is the plodder who beat the parade horse. \emph{La vaca} is the one who arrived unchanged and lent her name to medicine.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la vaca}
  \item \emph{el caballo}, then \emph{la vaca}
  \item \emph{la vaca del valle}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{vacca}? (A cow.) What does \emph{vaccinus} mean? (Of the cow.) And why is a vaccine called that? (The first one came from cowpox.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la oveja]{la oveja — the small one that ate the big one}

\label{lesson:ES-C296-oveja}



\begin{quote}
What kind of horse was a \emph{caballus}? (A plain work-horse.) And what is \emph{vaccinus}? (Of the cow.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la vaca — the animal before this one.
  \item la manta — often made of what this animal grows.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o-VE-ja}, stress in the middle. The \emph{j} is the scrape at the back of the mouth, the \emph{jota}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la oveja} — \textquotedblleft{}the sheep.\textquotedblright{}

Latin's word was \textbf{ovis}. Alongside it people used \textbf{ovicula}, with the ending that makes a thing small and fond — the ancestor of the \emph{-illo} and \emph{-ito} you can hear all over Spanish. \emph{Ovicula} meant something like \textquotedblleft{}little sheep.\textquotedblright{}

Then the odd thing. \emph{Ovis} died out completely, and the small fond version took over the whole job. Spanish has no word left that means \textquotedblleft{}sheep, full size, unsentimentally.\textquotedblright{} Every sheep is a little one now.

That happens more often than you would think. Latin \textbf{auricula}, a little ear, gave French \emph{oreille} and Spanish \emph{oreja} by exactly the same road — which is why \emph{oveja} and \emph{oreja} rhyme. The plain word for ear went the way of \emph{ovis}.

The English cousin stayed formal: \textbf{ovine} means \textquotedblleft{}of sheep,\textquotedblright{} and it comes straight from \emph{ovis}, the word Spanish threw away.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three animals, and a second rule to sit beside the first.

The plain word does not always win by staying plain. Sometimes it wins by shrinking: the affectionate version gets said so often that it stops sounding affectionate and simply becomes the word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la oveja}
  \item \emph{la vaca}, then \emph{la oveja}
  \item all three — \emph{el caballo}, \emph{la vaca}, \emph{la oveja}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{ovis}? (A sheep.) What did the \emph{-icula} ending do to it? (Made it small and fond.) And which of the two survived into Spanish? (The small one.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la gallina]{la gallina — the bird that is also an insult}

\label{lesson:ES-C296-gallina}



\begin{quote}
Three questions. Which horse won? (The plain one.) What is \emph{vaccinus}? (Of the cow.) And what did \emph{-icula} do to \emph{ovis}? (Made it small.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la oveja — the animal before this one.
  \item el huevo — what this one leaves you.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ga-LLI-na}, stress in the middle. The \emph{g} before \emph{a} is hard, and the \emph{ll} is a \emph{y}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la gallina} — \textquotedblleft{}the hen.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{gallus} was the cock, and \textbf{gallina} was made from it with the ending that marks the female. The pair came through intact: Spanish still has \emph{gallo} for the one and \emph{gallina} for the other.

English keeps \emph{gallina} only in its Sunday clothes. \textbf{Gallinaceous} is what a zoologist calls the whole family of birds that scratch about on the ground — hens, pheasants, turkeys. Nobody says it at breakfast.

The part worth having is not the bird. In Spanish, \emph{ser un gallina} — to be a hen — means to be a coward. English says \textbf{chicken} for exactly the same thing, and neither language borrowed the idea from the other. Two peoples watched the same animal and reached the same unkind conclusion.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four animals, and the first of them that carries an opinion.

\emph{El caballo}, \emph{la vaca} and \emph{la oveja} are only themselves. \emph{La gallina} is also a judgement about somebody, which makes it the first of the four you could be insulted with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la gallina}
  \item \emph{la oveja}, then \emph{la gallina}
  \item all four — \emph{el caballo}, \emph{la vaca}, \emph{la oveja}, \emph{la gallina}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{gallus}? (The cock.) What does \emph{gallinaceous} describe? (The whole ground-scratching family of birds.) And what does calling somebody \emph{un gallina} mean? (That they are a coward.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el burro]{el burro — the one English took whole}

\label{lesson:ES-C296-burro}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: which horse won, the grand one or the plain one? (The plain one.) What was \emph{ovis}? (A sheep.) And what does \emph{un gallina} call somebody? (A coward.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el caballo — what this one is the small, stubborn version of.
  \item la gallina — the animal before this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{BU-rro}, stress on the first part. The \emph{rr} is a full roll, not a single tap — the difference is real and it is the only difference here. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el burro} — \textquotedblleft{}the donkey.\textquotedblright{}

Behind it is late Latin \textbf{burricus}, a small horse, and behind that \textbf{burrus}, \textquotedblleft{}reddish\textquotedblright{} — the colour of the animal, borrowed by Latin from Greek. So a donkey is, quite literally, a little red horse. Which puts it in the same family as \emph{el caballo}, at a distance and going downhill.

Now the direction reverses. English did not inherit this word; it \textbf{borrowed} it, from Spanish speakers in the American southwest, and it borrowed it whole: \textbf{burro}, spelled and said the Spanish way. And then it borrowed the small version too. A \textbf{burrito} is a little donkey — nobody is certain why the food took the name, but the name is not a mystery at all once you have \emph{burro}.

That \emph{-ito} is the same ending you met flattening \emph{ovis} into \emph{oveja}, still at work and still making things small.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{el caballo}, \emph{la vaca}, \emph{la oveja}, \emph{la gallina}, \emph{el burro}.

Read in order they are a farmyard, and they arrived by four different routes: a word that beat its own posh rival, a word that barely changed, a word that only survived by shrinking, a pair kept together, and a word English took back off Spanish long after Latin had finished with it.

Traffic in words is not one-way, and this run ends on the one going the other direction.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el burro}
  \item \emph{el caballo}, then \emph{el burro} — the horse and the little red one
  \item all five — \emph{el caballo}, \emph{la vaca}, \emph{la oveja}, \emph{la gallina}, \emph{el burro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{burrus} mean? (Reddish.) Which language took \emph{burro} from which? (English took it from Spanish.) And what is a \emph{burrito}, taken literally? (A little donkey.)
\end{tcolorbox}
